headline: Request parsers that stalled on a run of spaces run in linear time, a client address means one client however it is spelled, the NTS client works against a real server, and an algorithm label has to match the key that does the work
summary:
Nine regular expressions on request-facing paths backtracked on a long run of whitespace. The `b.middleware.scimServer` filter parser spent about 8.7 seconds of synchronous CPU on a 4 KiB query string, with no credentials needed when `bearer` is unset, and the prompt-injection classifier in `b.ai.input` spent 1.6 seconds on one 64 KiB input. `b.guardRegex.assertSafe`, which screens the patterns an operator passes to `b.forms`, `b.middleware.cors` and a dozen other primitives, accepted the same shapes and their lookahead spellings. Every one of those expressions now runs in linear time, the screen refuses the shapes, and each consumer screens the pattern it actually runs.

A dual-stack listener reports an IPv4 client as `::ffff:a.b.c.d`. `b.middleware.networkAllowlist` compared that text against its CIDRs, so `deniedCidrs: ["10.0.0.0/8"]` did not deny `::ffff:10.0.0.1`, and a malformed CIDR such as `10.0.0.0/33` matched nothing. `b.ssrfGuard.createAllowlist`, rate-limit keys, session fingerprints, the mail RBL and greylist checks and several other comparisons had the same gap. Every one of them now compares addresses in canonical form and refuses a malformed entry when it is built.

The NTS client offered AES-128-GCM-SIV under the name ChaCha20-Poly1305 (codepoint 30 where the registry assigns 29), sent an IP address as TLS SNI, which Node 26 refuses, and accepted an authenticated reply from a server that reported itself unsynchronized. It now runs against chrony in the test stack. Checking every protocol codepoint table in the framework against its registry found eight more wrong values; one of them put C2PA timestamps under a COSE label no verifier reads.

Several primitives wrote an algorithm name taken from a default or an option while the key passed in decided the operation. `b.crypto.encrypt` labeled an envelope ML-KEM-1024 when it was handed an RSA key. Every such primitive now checks the key against the name it writes. A `b.router` TLS listener ran on OpenSSL's default key-exchange groups, so a client that listed X25519 first negotiated X25519 behind `b.pqcGate`.

Several changes refuse input that was accepted before, and some names are removed. The Migration section lists what to change.

items.title: `b.middleware.scimServer` parses a filter in linear time
items.body: A filter of `a eq`, a few thousand spaces and an encoded line break made the filter expression backtrack cubically: a 4 KiB URL held the event loop for about 8.7 seconds, and with `bearer` unset the request needed no credentials. The filter is trimmed and matched by an expression with one quantifier per whitespace run. Filter operators are case-insensitive, as RFC 7644 section 3.4.2.2 requires, so `userName Eq "x"` parses as `eq`.

items.title: `b.ai.input` classifies a hostile prompt in linear time
items.body: `you are` followed by 64 KiB of spaces cost 1.6 seconds of synchronous CPU in `b.ai.input.classify`, and `classifyWithSources` classifies up to 64 such sources per call. The act-as-different-system pattern now gives each whitespace run to one quantifier. Detection of `you are [now | from now on] a/an X` is unchanged.

items.title: `b.guardRegex.assertSafe` refuses patterns that backtrack quadratically or cubically, and judges a pattern the way its consumer runs it
items.body: Two adjacent repetitions that share a character pass only when one term on its own matches every remaining character. The screen used to union the character sets of every term after the pair, which cleared shapes such as `^key:\s+(.+)$` and `a\s+(.+)\s*` that cost seconds on a few kilobytes. A lookahead or lookbehind after a repetition is judged as the second half of a pair, so `^(.*?)(?=\s*$)` is refused, and so are `^.+@.+$` and `^.*a.*$`, where a required character both halves can match does not fix the split. The `v` flag is judged as `u`. The end of a pattern counts as an end anchor only when the consumer anchors it: `b.forms` and `b.middleware.cors` screen the `^(?:pattern)$` form they run, while a search consumer (JSON Schema `pattern`, JSONPath `search()`, `b.middleware.botGuard` agents, request-log `skipPaths`) keeps linear patterns such as `^Bearer\s+(.+)` that it accepted before. A pattern refused now throws at configuration time.

items.title: Client addresses are compared in canonical form
items.body: `b.middleware.networkAllowlist` denies an IPv4 client that a dual-stack listener reports as `::ffff:a.b.c.d`, its hex spelling, and a NAT64 (`64:ff9b::/96`) or 6to4 (`2002::/16`) address carrying a denied IPv4 address; an IPv6 deny entry that contains `::ffff:0:0/96` denies every IPv4 client. `b.requestHelpers.clientIp`, `trustedClientIp().resolve` and `extractActorContext` return canonical addresses, so rate-limit keys, session fingerprints, break-glass IP pins, per-IP static quotas and audit actor fields treat one client as one address. `ipKey` and `ipPrefix` key NAT64 and 6to4 clients on the IPv4 address they carry; before, every such client shared one bucket. `trustedProxies`, `b.pqcGate` `bypass`, NO_PROXY, `b.mail.greylist` `allowedSources` and MX relay CIDRs match every spelling.

items.title: `b.ssrfGuard.createAllowlist` matches every spelling of an address
items.body: A URL host such as `[fd00::5]` keeps its brackets, and the allowlist compared that text against IPv6 CIDRs, so a deny entry such as `fd00::/8` did not block `http://[fd00::5]/`. Hosts and entries are compared by address: an IPv4-mapped CIDR matches both spellings, an IPv4 deny entry also blocks the `::ffff:`, 6to4 and NAT64 spellings of a denied address, and deny entries also apply to every address an allowed host name resolves to (`ssrf-guard/on-denylist` with `err.ip`). `b.ssrfGuard.canonicalizeHost` reads an address with a zone id from the text before the `%`, so `::ffff:10.0.0.1%eth0` is `10.0.0.1` rather than `0.0.0.0`.

items.title: A `b.router` TLS listener negotiates a post-quantum group when the client offers one
items.body: When `tlsOptions` carries no `ecdhCurve`, `listen()` sets the listener's groups to `b.network.tls.serverKeyAgreementGroups()`, read when `listen()` runs. Before, the listener used OpenSSL's default list, and a client offering `X25519:SecP256r1MLKEM768` negotiated X25519, including behind `b.pqcGate`. An `ecdhCurve` you set is kept, and the returned server carries it as `keyAgreementGroups`. `b.network.tls.applyToContext()` writes the same server tuples for a listener, and takes `role: "client"` for an outbound agent.

items.title: `b.pqcGate` requires a ClientHello that can reach TLS 1.3
items.body: A TLS 1.2 handshake through the gate negotiated classical ECDHE even when the ClientHello listed a post-quantum group. The gate now requires `supported_versions` to list TLS 1.3, refuses a ClientHello that repeats `supported_groups` or `supported_versions` or whose list lengths disagree with their extensions, and counts a post-quantum group only when it sits in a tuple ahead of every classical group of the listener's group string. `b.pqcGate.acceptedGroupIds()` reports the groups it counts.

items.title: `b.crypto.encrypt` and `b.crypto.decrypt` refuse a key of the wrong type
items.body: An RSA, X25519, ML-KEM-512 or ML-KEM-768 key produced and opened an envelope whose header named ML-KEM-1024. Both now throw `crypto/key-type-mismatch` (`b.crypto.CryptoKeyError`) unless the key is the type the envelope's KEM id names: ML-KEM-1024 for the default and KEM-only suites, ML-KEM-768 for `encryptMlkem768X25519`, EC P-384 or X25519 for the classical halves. `b.crypto.hpke.seal` and `open` refuse anything but ML-KEM-1024 with `crypto-hpke/bad-key`.

items.title: A signature label must match the signing key
items.body: `b.vc.issue`, `b.auth.sdJwtVc.issue` and `present`, `b.auth.dpop.buildProof`, `b.middleware.protectedResourceMetadata`, `b.mail.arc.sign`, `b.mail.dkim.create`, SAML signing, the GCS object store, `b.mcp.toolRegistry.create`, `b.webhook.signer` with `pqc-pem`, `b.webPush.buildVapidAuthHeader`, `b.contentCredentials.signCose` and `b.auditSign.init` now refuse a key whose type, curve or parameter set does not match the algorithm they write. Before, each wrote the configured name over a signature made with whatever key was passed.

items.title: The outbound DLP sees what is sent
items.body: `b.redact.installOutboundDlp` missed a card number written as a JSON number (`{"card":4111111111111111}`), with a fraction or exponent (`4111111111111111110.0`), behind a JSON escape in an httpClient text body (`"\u0034111..."`), as a member name, a header name or a URL part, in a multipart field or in-memory file, after an earlier digit run in the same string, and in a body a `before` hook rewrote. Each is now classified. A member name, header name or URL part that would need redacting refuses the request. A webhook body sent as a JSON string is also scanned for the values its parsed form loses (integers beyond 2^53, duplicate member names, `__proto__` members), and a JSON body over the parser's limits is scanned token by token in bounded memory. A bytes body was always read as UTF-8, so a UTF-16 body hid a card number behind NUL bytes; it is now read as UTF-8 and in the encoding its byte-order mark or `Content-Type` charset names. A body that cannot be decoded (a UTF-32 byte-order mark, an unknown charset, a UTF-16 charset with no byte order) is refused with `redact-dlp/undecodable-body`, and a redaction that would have to re-encode a non-UTF-8 body refuses the request.

items.title: Logs and audit rows do not carry secrets in member names or bound fields
items.body: `b.redact.redact` checked member names only against its sensitive-name list, so `{"4111111111111111": 1}` reached `b.log` lines and `b.audit.safeEmit` rows unchanged. A member name that matches a value detector is now written as the marker, numbered `[REDACTED:2]`, `[REDACTED:3]` within one object, with key order kept. `b.log` passed only per-call extras through the redactor; `base`, `.bind()` and `.runWithContext()` fields now go through it too. When redaction throws, `b.audit.safeEmit` wrote the original actor, reason and metadata; it now writes the row with an empty actor and the marker in place of the reason and metadata.

items.title: `b.router` and `b.middleware.composePipeline` honor `next()` once per middleware
items.body: The `next` handed to a middleware wrote into state shared by the whole loop, so a second or delayed `next()` let a request past a later middleware that never called `next`, such as an authorization gate. `next` now counts only until the middleware's own turn settles. A middleware that calls `next()` and then throws does not advance the chain a second time.

items.title: The NTS client follows RFC 8915 and the IANA AEAD registry
items.body: `b.network.ntp.nts.AEAD_CHACHA20_POLY1305` is 29; it was 30, which is AES-128-GCM-SIV, so a server that picked 30 from the old offer failed every query. The default offer is `[15, 29]`. A KE response is checked for its Next Protocol and AEAD records, unrecognized critical records and Warning records; a reply from an unsynchronized server fails as `nts/unsynchronized`; unauthenticated or off-source datagrams are discarded while the query keeps waiting; era-1 timestamps (after February 2036) read correctly; a response split across TLS records is accepted. `opts.aead`, `servername`, `host` and `timeoutMs` are validated before a socket opens.

items.title: An IP address is no longer sent as TLS SNI
items.body: Node 26 refuses an IP address as a TLS server name, so the NTS client, DNS over TLS (including the `BLAMEJS_DNS_TRANSPORT=dot` default of 1.1.1.1), `b.network.proxy`, the OTLP gRPC log stream, `b.network.tls.buildOptions` and `b.network.tls.connectWithEch` failed against an address. `b.network.tls.sniFor()` returns the name to send, and `b.network.tls.identityFor()` answers which name the certificate is checked against; a `servername` that is an IP address other than the host is refused when the client is built.

items.title: An IPv6 address written in brackets is dialed and verified as the address
items.body: A URL keeps the brackets on an IPv6 host. Passing `[::1]` as a connect host made certificate verification fail with `ERR_TLS_CERT_ALTNAME_INVALID` in `b.httpClient`, DNS over HTTPS, `b.wsClient` and the Redis client, and made `b.router` listen, `b.mail.server` listeners, `b.network.heartbeat` tcp targets and the `b.pqcGate` `internalHost` fail with `ENOTFOUND` on Linux. Every dial and listen site strips the brackets.

items.title: `b.mail.rbl` no longer refuses every IPv4 sender on a dual-stack MX
items.body: `b.mail.rbl` threw `mail-rbl/bad-input` for `::ffff:a.b.c.d`, so an MX listening on `::` with an RBL gate answered 421 to every IPv4 sender. It looks the sender up under its IPv4 address, as do SPF, iprev and HELO checks.

items.title: C2PA timestamps are written where C2PA verifiers read them
items.body: `b.contentCredentials.signCose` put the RFC 3161 token under COSE label 35, which is `x5u`, so c2patool and other verifiers saw no timestamp. It is written under the text label `sigTst2` as `{ tstTokens: [ { val } ] }`, over the C2PA v2 CounterSignature structure, and `x5chain` is in the protected header. `verifyCose` reads the token only from `sigTst2`. A malformed container fails as `timestamp-invalid:sigtst2-malformed`, and a token under label 35 fails as `timestamp-invalid:legacy-label-35`.

items.title: `b.mail.bimi` tells a Common Mark Certificate from a Verified Mark Certificate
items.body: CMC detection keyed on OID 1.3.6.1.4.1.53087.1.2, which a real CMC does not carry, so every CMC was reported as `vmc`. `fetchAndVerifyMark` takes the type from the leaf's `markType` attribute, returns `markType`, and requires the Mark Certificate General Policy Identifier 1.3.6.1.4.1.53087.1.1.

items.title: `b.crypto.hpke.pq.connolly` and `.wg` speak RFC 9180 HPKE
items.body: Both wrappers were documented as interoperating with the drafts they name, but they wrapped the blamejs sealing format. They now implement the RFC 9180 key schedule under the IANA HPKE codepoints with ML-KEM-1024 (and MLKEM1024-P384 on `wg`), pinned by the draft-ietf-hpke-pq-05 test vectors, with psk mode and the multi-message `setupSender` / `setupRecipient` context. `b.crypto.hpke` keeps its wire format and is documented as a blamejs format with no RFC 9180 interoperability; its `SUPPORTED_SUITE.aead` now reads `XChaCha20-Poly1305`, the cipher the format has always used.

items.title: Registry codepoints corrected
items.body: `b.websocket` accepts the registered close codes 1012 to 1014 and refuses 1004 to 1006, 1015 and 1016 to 2999 on send and receive. `b.network.dns.classifyDnskeyAlgorithm` knows algorithms 0, 17, 18 and 23. TSIG writes the registered name `HMAC-MD5.SIG-ALG.REG.INT`, so legacy MD5 TSIG works with BIND, Knot and PowerDNS. `b.constants.PQC_GROUPS` lists the pure ML-KEM groups, and `b.pqcAgent` accepts MLKEM768 and MLKEM1024.

items.title: `b.externalDb` disposes a client whose setup failed and runs a transaction on its own backend
items.body: `b.externalDb.adapters.connectAs` leaked the client when a `SET ROLE` or GUC statement failed, so each failure held a pool slot until every later query hung; it now disposes the client (`close(client, err)` replaces the default). With more than one backend, the default BEGIN, COMMIT and ROLLBACK ran through the last declared backend's query function; each backend now uses its own.

items.title: An async transaction body or migration step is refused instead of committed half-run
items.body: `b.db.transaction`, `b.migrations` and `b.db.init({ migrationDir })` committed as soon as the callback returned, so an async body was recorded as applied while it was still running outside the transaction. An async function is refused with `db/async-transaction-fn` or `migrations/up-failed` before it runs; a plain function that returns a promise is rolled back.

items.title: `b.mail.server.imap` parses SELECT and EXAMINE parameters by the RFC 7162 grammar
items.body: A parameter list the old expression did not recognize, including the seq-match-data form of QRESYNC, was passed to the store as part of the mailbox name. `(CONDSTORE)` and every QRESYNC form now parse, and any other trailing text is answered BAD. STORE with UNCHANGEDSINCE and APPEND with CATENATE no longer backtrack on a long line.

items.title: A proxied request and an ECH dial report a bad TLS option instead of crashing or hanging
items.body: An https request through `b.network.proxy` with a key, certificate or pfx that Node cannot load threw from the CONNECT reply handler and crashed the process; it now emits `error` on the request and closes the tunnel. `b.network.tls.connectWithEch` to a host name with a `ca` entry that is not a string or Buffer never settled; it now rejects once with `network-tls/bad-tls-options`.

items.title: `b.httpClient` waits for a `before` hook that returns a promise
items.body: The `before` option was documented as `(opts) => opts | Promise`, but the request used the promise itself as its options and failed with `url is required`. The next hook and the request now receive the resolved options, in order, and a rejected promise rejects the request with `http-client/before-threw`.

items.title: Body parsers and storage calls check the options they are given
items.body: `b.middleware.bodyParser`, `b.parsers.json` and `b.parsers.multipart` validate every option when built or called and throw `body-parser/bad-*` codes for a non-numeric cap, a non-function `fileFilter` or a string `mimeAllowlist`. Multipart `maxBytes` counts every byte up to the closing boundary and refuses with `body-parser/multipart-total-too-large`, and a part header block over 16 KiB is refused even when it arrives in one chunk. Every `b.storage` per-call primitive refuses an option it does not read with `storage/bad-opts`, and `b.storage.presignedDownloadUrl` refuses `responseHeaders` on a backend that is not SigV4, which signed the URL without them. The SAML logout builders and `verifyResponse` raise `auth-saml/bad-signing-key` and `auth-saml/bad-idp-cert` for a key or certificate they cannot read, which used to escape as raw OpenSSL errors.

items.title: Smaller fixes
items.body: `b.network.tls.preferredGroups.set` refuses a name that is not a TLS 1.3 group or that the runtime OpenSSL cannot set, naming it in `tls/bad-key-share`, instead of failing at the next `listen()`. `b.guardCidr` accepts IPv6 with a dotted IPv4 tail, checks the IPv4 address embedded under `::ffff:0:0/96`, `64:ff9b::/96`, the deprecated `::/96` and `::ffff:0:0:0/96`, and reports every block the IANA special-purpose registries mark not globally reachable. `b.mtlsEngine.canVerifyInTls` answers correctly under a narrowed post-quantum posture. `b.cms.parseSignedData` throws `cms/bad-signer-info` for a short SignerInfo. `b.observability` OTLP export keeps each span under its own instrumentation scope. The syslog sink resolves a `udp://` host on each emit and uses the address family it resolves to. The cluster pubsub warning names the row that failed. The Redis client clears its connect timer when the TLS dial fails synchronously.

items.title: Vendored `@blamejs/pki` 0.9.5 and the 2026-10-17 public suffix list
items.body: `@blamejs/pki` 0.9.5 refuses a non-boolean value for a switch option (for example `detached: "false"` in `pki.cms.sign`, or `protectHeaders` in `pki.smime.sign`) instead of reading it as the opposite of what it says; `null` and an omitted option still select the default. The public suffix list is the 2026-10-17_18-52-06_UTC edition.

items.title: New primitives
items.body: `b.network.tls.sniFor(host)`, `b.network.tls.identityFor(host, servername?, opts?)`, `b.crypto.assertKeyType(key, accepted, opts?)`, `b.websocket.isValidCloseCode(code)`, `b.pqcGate.acceptedGroupIds(groups?)`, `b.crypto.hpke.pq.connolly.setupSender` / `setupRecipient` / `generateKeyPair` and the same on `.wg`, `b.mail.bimi.MC_GENERAL_POLICY_OID` and `b.mail.bimi.MARK_TYPE_OID`. The server `b.router` `listen()` returns carries a read-only `keyAgreementGroups`.

items.title: SLH-DSA algorithms in `b.contentCredentials`
items.body: COSE has no registered codepoint for SLH-DSA; the values the framework wrote belonged to other algorithms. `slh-dsa-sha2-128s` and `slh-dsa-shake-256f` are refused with `content-credentials/bad-alg`.

items.title: `VMC_POLICY_OID` and `CMC_POLICY_OID` on `b.mail.bimi`
items.body: Use `b.mail.bimi.MC_GENERAL_POLICY_OID` (the same value as the old `VMC_POLICY_OID`) and `b.mail.bimi.MARK_TYPE_OID`. The CMC policy OID had no counterpart in the Mark Certificate requirements.

items.title: Options and codes that nothing read
items.body: `audit-only` in `shadowRegistry` `onCardinalityExceeded` behaved exactly like `drop` and now throws `metrics-shadow/bad-policy`. The `b.storage` presign option `expiresInSec` was never read and is refused; use `expiresIn` (seconds, default 900, 1 to 604800). The `body-parser/multipart-too-large` code is removed in favor of `body-parser/multipart-total-too-large`. The NTS handshake result no longer carries `warnings`, since a Warning record now fails the handshake.

items.title: The framework's own regular expressions are probed at every repeatable token
items.body: The linearity gate built its probe text from a literal prefix and stopped at the first quantifier, so no probe reached a pair of quantifiers behind an earlier one. It now walks each pattern and builds a probe at every repeatable token, with multi-character tails, and measures every pattern in a child process under a deadline.

items.title: Protocol codepoint tables are pinned to their registries
items.body: A table carrying a `// registry: <url>` line must be checked in `registry-codepoints.test.js` against a transcription of that registry; each test used to build its fixture from the constant it was testing.

items.title: Loop closures, raw SNI, bracketed hosts, address comparisons, listener groups and KEM key types
items.body: eslint `no-loop-func` is on for `lib/`. The pattern gate refuses a TLS `servername` taken from a raw host, a connect host taken from a URL's `hostname` without removing brackets, an address-to-CIDR comparison outside the shared canonical matcher, a TLS listener built without the server group tuples, a KEM call with no key-type check in the same function, and an options parameter defaulted and never read.

items.title: Re-seal data sealed with `b.crypto.hpke.pq.connolly` or `.wg`
items.body: Envelopes sealed by these wrappers in 0.10.10 through 0.21.2 do not open in 0.21.3, and the reverse holds. Their errors now carry `crypto-hpke-pq/*` codes, their audit rows are `system.hpke.pq.*`, and their metrics are `hpke.pq.seal`, `hpke.pq.open` and `hpke.pq.setup` labeled `{ outcome, draft }`.

items.title: Re-sign manifests and tool descriptors whose signatures change
items.body: `b.contentCredentials.verifyCose` does not read the timestamp `signCose` wrote under COSE label 35 in 0.21.2 and earlier: such a manifest returns `valid: false` with `reason: "timestamp-invalid:legacy-label-35"` whatever `requireTimestamp` is set to. Re-sign it with `signCose`, which writes the token under `sigTst2`. `signCose` defaults to `ml-dsa-87` and refuses other key types, so pass `alg` for Ed25519, ECDSA or ML-DSA-44/65 keys. `b.mcp.toolRegistry` `es384` and `es512` now hash with SHA-384 and SHA-512, so descriptors signed earlier under those algorithms no longer verify.

items.title: Sessions from IPv4 clients on a dual-stack listener re-fingerprint once
items.body: `b.session` stores the fingerprint only when a session is created or rotated. An existing session from an IPv4 client on a dual-stack listener was fingerprinted on `::ffff:a.b.c.d` and is now compared against `a.b.c.d`, so it reports `fingerprintDrift` and emits `auth.session.fingerprint_drift` on every verify until it rotates or expires. With `requireFingerprintMatch: true`, or with `maxAnomalyScore` set, verify returns null and those users sign in again once. `b.sessionDeviceBinding` is not affected.

items.title: Check keys handed to signing and encryption primitives
items.body: A key that does not match the configured algorithm now throws instead of producing a mislabeled signature or envelope. `b.auditSign.init` refuses a key file whose keys are not a pair or do not match its `algorithm`. `b.auth.sdJwtVc` without an `algorithm` takes it from the key and refuses P-521, ML-DSA-44 and RSA. `b.auth.dpop.buildProof` refuses an `opts.jwk` that is not the public half of `privateKey`.

items.title: Rewrite operator patterns that `b.guardRegex.assertSafe` now refuses
items.body: A pattern such as `^\w+\s*=\s*.*$`, `^key:\s+(.+)$` or `^.+@.+$` throws at configuration time. Equivalent accepted forms are `^\w+\s*=\s*(?:\S.*)?$`, `^key:\s+\S.*$`, `^[^@]+@[^@]+$`, or a greedy `[\s\S]*` in place of the overlapping pair.

items.title: Fix allowlist and CIDR entries that never matched
items.body: `b.middleware.networkAllowlist` refuses `10.0.0.0/33`, `10.0.0/8`, `010.0.0.0/8`, `10.0.0.0/8x` and a `deniedCidrs` that is not an array with `network-allowlist/bad-opt`; each used to match nothing. `b.ssrfGuard.createAllowlist` refuses unknown options, a malformed CIDR and a host the URL parser reads differently (`api.example.com:443`, `10.0.0`) with `ssrf-guard/bad-entry`. A malformed `trustedProxies` CIDR and a malformed `b.pqcGate` `bypass` entry throw `TypeError`.

items.title: Expect redacted member names in logs and refused non-UTF-8 bodies
items.body: A log or audit consumer that reads a member whose name was a card number, an SSN, a JWT or another detected value finds it under `[REDACTED]` or a numbered `[REDACTED:n]`; a 9-digit name and a Luhn-valid 13 to 19 digit name, which includes a millisecond timestamp used as a key, are renamed the same way. An outbound body whose bytes cannot be decoded is refused, a string body sent under `charset=us-ascii` or `iso-8859-1` that needs a redaction is refused rather than sent redacted, and a UTF-16 body with neither a byte-order mark nor a charset is still read only as UTF-8. The message string of a `b.log` line is written as given.

items.title: Make transaction bodies and migration steps synchronous
items.body: An async function passed to `b.db.transaction`, or an async `up` or `down` step, is refused. The framework database API is synchronous; do the asynchronous work before or after the transaction.

items.title: Listeners behind `b.pqcGate` must reach TLS 1.3
items.body: A listener with `maxVersion` below TLSv1.3 or a version-pinned `secureProtocol` cannot be gated. A listener given its own `ecdhCurve` passes its group string to the gate, `b.pqcGate.create({ groups: server.keyAgreementGroups })`. A listener configured outside `b.router` takes its options from `b.network.tls.applyToContext({ base })`; an outbound agent uses `applyToContext({ base, role: "client" })`.

items.title: Other refusals
items.body: `b.wsClient` `send(data)` throws `ws-client/bad-opt` for a second argument. `close(code)` on a `b.websocket` connection or a `b.wsClient` sends 1000 only when `code` is omitted; an explicit `0`, `null`, a numeric string or a fraction throws `TypeError`. `b.backup.create` requires `flushBeforeBackup` to be `false`, a function, or omitted. `b.network.tls.preferredGroups.set` refuses `auto`, `DEFAULT` and groups the runtime cannot set. IMAP `SELECT` with unrecognized trailing text is answered BAD. A `servername` that is an IP address other than the host is refused by the SMTP transport, the Redis client, `b.wsClient` and the syslog sink. `b.middleware.bodyParser` and `b.storage` refuse options they do not read.
